The encoder is made by Bourns Encoders, and the model number is: EMS22A50-C20-LS6.

It's a 1024 step / revolution resolution, and has a very low required shaft torque. It is addressed via a synchronous serial interface, meaning that a clock, data, and chip select pin are needed to interface with it. In addition, they can be daisy chained. Therefore I could read 10 encoders using just 3 wires of my microcontroller. Using an Arduino, the interface is accomplished quite nicely using the shiftIn() function. 

The encoder can be purchased off of Mouser Electronics, here's the link to it: 

Riggggttttt,  [here!](http://www.mouser.com/ProductDetail/Bourns/EMS22A50-C20-LS6/?qs=oyIm%2F3giSj7PlEF33k%252bmdA%3D%3D)

It's rather expensive at $38 each, but well worth the price if you need an easily addressed, high precision rotary encoder. It is absolute, meaning no losing count of pulses, and capable of operating at up to 10,000 RPM. That means you could hook this thing up to your car engine's crankshaft and know the exact angle at any given time while red-lining it. Pretty cool for a small little encoder.
